deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT. The page continues the previous page's note. That note says that as the '24th problem' of his Paris lecture (1900) Hilbert had wanted to pose criteria for the simplicity of proofs, and a theory of proof methods. Dating: shortly after 1900.

PART 1 (simplicity of proofs, continued). Knowing a syzygy considerably simplifies the proof that a given identity holds. Each elementary step of a computation (an addition, an application of the commutative law of addition, etc.) corresponds to a geometric theorem or a logical inference. So one can count these steps. For particular theorems of elementary geometry (Pythagoras, the notable points of a triangle) one can then decide which proof is the simplest. There is no derivation. It is a programmatic proposal: a complexity measure for proofs given by the number of elementary inference or computation steps, i.e. proof length.

PART 2 (programme). 'Make out of differential geometry an integral geometry, and out of differential physics an integral physics.' That is, study how the whole course of functions, bendings (Verbiegung) of surfaces, flows, etc. behaves in the whole of space. In modern terms this is global analysis, i.e. differential geometry and PDE 'im Grossen', as opposed to local theory. This is not Blaschke's later 'Integralgeometrie' (geometric probability, Crofton formulas).

PART 3 (uniqueness theorem).
Claim: let f, g be continuous on [0,1]. Define
  I_1[f] = ∫_0^1 f(x) dx,
  I_2[f] = ∫_0^1 ∫_0^x f,
  I_3[f] = ∫_0^1 ∫_0^x ∫_0^{x'} f,
  and so on.
If I_k[f] = I_k[g] for all k, then f = g.

Step (mine, standard): by Cauchy's formula for repeated integration,
  I_k[f] = ∫_0^1 (1-t)^{k-1}/(k-1)! · f(t) dt.
So the data are equivalent to all moments ∫_0^1 t^m f(t) dt, m ≥ 0.

Proof 1 (Hilbert). Expand f in Legendre polynomials ('Kugelfunctionen X_n', here necessarily shifted to [0,1]). Each coefficient ∫ X_n f dx is a finite linear combination of the I_k. This follows by repeated partial integration. Write F_1(x) = ∫_0^x f and F_{j+1}(x) = ∫_0^x F_j. For a polynomial P of degree n:
  ∫_0^1 P f = Σ_{j=0}^{n} (-1)^j P^{(j)}(1) F_{j+1}(1),
  with F_{j+1}(1) = I_{j+1}.
Example (mine): ∫_0^1 (2x-1) f dx = I_1 - 2 I_2.
Hence the Legendre coefficients of f and g agree. Implicit step (mine): this forces f = g by completeness of the Legendre system for continuous functions, e.g. via Weierstrass approximation or Parseval: h = f - g is orthogonal to all polynomials, so ∫ h^2 = 0.

Proof 2 (sketch, 'Oder auch'). Take a polynomial f(x) = a_0 + a_1 x + ... + a_n x^n. Compute I_1[f] and I_2[f] as linear forms in the a_k. Then represent f formally as
  f(x) = φ_1(x) I_1[f] + φ_2(x) I_2[f] + φ_3(x) I_3[f] + ...
That is an expansion with respect to a system φ_k biorthogonal to the functionals I_k. It is left as a formal sketch.
errors: The coefficients in the polynomial formulas are wrong. Correct: ∫_0^1 f = a_0 + a_1/2 + a_2/3 + ... + a_n/(n+1). Hilbert wrote a_2/2 and a_n/n.

Double integral slip. Correct: ∫_0^1∫_0^x f = a_0/2 + a_1/6 + a_2/12 + ... + a_n/((n+1)(n+2)). Hilbert wrote a_0 + a_1/2! + a_2/(3·2) + ... + a_n/(n(n-1)), so the denominators are shifted by one or two places.
The triple integral is written ∫_0^1∫_0^x∫_0^x. The inner upper limit should be a new variable (x'), which is clearly the intention.
Kugelfunctionen X_n normally live on [-1,1]. For integrals over [0,1] one needs shifted Legendre polynomials. This is minor and implicit.
Proof 1 silently uses completeness of the Legendre system (equivalently, Weierstrass approximation). The argument is correct, but this step is unstated.

The final expansion f = Σ φ_k I_k[f] is only formal. The φ_k are not specified. Biorthogonal expansions against the non-orthogonal system (1-t)^{k-1}/(k-1)! need not converge for general continuous f without regrouping, as in the Legendre route. The step is unjustified as written.

results.what: Proposal to measure the simplicity of proofs by counting elementary operations or inferences, and to determine the simplest proof (the '24th problem')
results.modern_name: Hilbert's 24th problem; proof complexity / proof length; proof theory
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert himself; the note was rediscovered and published by R. Thiele (2000, Amer. Math. Monthly 2003); modern proof complexity from the 1970s onward

results.what: Programme: replace local (differential) geometry and physics by global ('integral') study of functions, bendings and flows in the whole space
results.modern_name: Global differential geometry / global analysis ('im Grossen')
results.usually_credited_to: Hilbert (1901 nonexistence of complete surfaces of constant negative curvature), Blaschke, Hopf, Cohn-Vossen and others in the 1920s-30s

results.what: A continuous function on [0,1] is determined by all its iterated integrals from 0 to 1, equivalently by all its moments
results.modern_name: Uniqueness in the Hausdorff moment problem / Lerch's theorem (vanishing moments imply f = 0)
results.usually_credited_to: Consequence of Weierstrass approximation (1885); Lerch (1892/1903); Stieltjes (1894); Hausdorff (1921)

results.what: Expressing Legendre coefficients through iterated integrals by repeated integration by parts
results.modern_name: Cauchy repeated-integration formula plus integration by parts

deep.surprise_reason: The 24th-problem note on this and the previous page is already famous and published (Thiele 2000/2003). The moment-uniqueness argument is routine for c. 1900 and contains computational slips. The 'integral geometry' remark is a programmatic aside consistent with Hilbert's known global-geometry work.
